title: Book Review: Tom Vickers, Organizing Amazon: Building Worker Power under Conditions of Fragmentation, Precarity and Regimentation VickersTomOrganizing Amazon: Building Worker Power under Conditions of Fragmentation, Precarity and RegimentationBristol: Bristol University Press, 2025, £14.99 (ISBN: 978-1529254297), 160 pp.
The Chains That Bind? Restrictive Covenants and Labor Market Entrants' Perceived Occupational Mobility
affiliations: University of Southampton and Hertie School Berlin Southampton Hampshire UK; Bangko Sentral Ng Pilipinas and Ateneo de Manila University Manila Philippines
abstract: ABSTRACT Using a conjoint experiment on highly educated labor market entrants in the Philippines, we examine how restrictive covenants shape perceived occupational mobility. Respondents compared hypothetical jobseeker profiles with randomized non‐compete, training repayment, and non‐solicitation clauses, then chose the likely applicant to four mobility pathways: vertical or lateral jobs within or across industries. Findings show that non‐compete clauses deter within‐industry and encourage across‐industry perceived mobility. Training repayment and non‐solicitation clauses exert targeted effects depending on scope conditions. Finally, these patterns hold across contractual breadth and firms' monitoring stringency, and are attenuated by positive beliefs about loyalty norms and perceived sufficiency of legal recourse.
journal: Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society

title: Sex and the City: Demographics, Spatial Sorting, and the Marriage Market
authors: Min Fang; Zibin Huang; Yushi Wang; Yu (Alan) Yang
affiliations: Department of Economics and Decision Sciences China Europe International Business School Pudong Shanghai China; Lanzillotti Public Policy Research Center University of Florida Gainesville Florida USA; College of Business Shanghai University of Finance and Economics Shanghai China; Shanghai Institute of International Finance and Economics Shanghai China; International Business School Hainan University Haikou China; Guanghua School of Management Peking University Beijing China
abstract: ABSTRACT We study how the interaction between demographic changes and spatial sorting affects marriage matching across space. Using data from China, we first present stylized facts on the diverging spatial distribution of singlehood characterized by a high singles rate for females (males) in more (less) developed cities. We then build a quantitative spatial equilibrium model. It reveals that more highly educated women sort into the service sector in more developed cities than men. With persistent social norms of hypergamy, this results in more failed marriage matches for females (males) in more (less) developed cities, thereby lowering the national marriage rate.
